definition: Egalitarian means holding that all people deserve equal rights, status, and opportunity — or built so that they actually get them.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word egalitarian. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know egalitarian should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The chess club stayed stubbornly egalitarian: grandmaster or beginner, every member waited in the same signup line for a board.

Fair-minded is milder than egalitarian: a fair-minded person plays no favorites in the matter at hand, while an egalitarian holds the sweeping conviction that everyone deserves equal standing everywhere.
Leveling goes further than egalitarian: an egalitarian wants equal rights and equal worth recognized, while a leveling program sets out to erase distinctions of rank and wealth altogether.

The op-ed asked whether the new bus routes were truly equitable when three neighborhoods lost service and one gained it.
Egalitarian means holding that all people deserve equal rights, status, and opportunity — or built so that they actually get them.

The new director made the orchestra egalitarian in a single season: auditions moved behind a screen, every chair rotated monthly, and the last stand of the violas drew the same rehearsal solos as the concertmaster.
Notice what the word claims: not that the players are identical in skill, but that the institution levels their standing — equal access, equal voice, equal treatment.
An egalitarian arrangement is about the worth people are granted, not the sameness of what they can do.
Egalitarian pledges more than niceness: it asserts that people deserve equal standing, and it usually describes arrangements — charters, pay scales, institutions — or the people who fight for them.
It is not a synonym for generous, and it is not about matching objects: a gift can be lavish without being egalitarian, and identical houses make a street uniform, not equal.
When rank is earned and celebrated, the right word is meritocratic — and an egalitarian would still object.

When Ines founded her mapping startup, she wrote an unusual rule into the charter: every employee, herself included, would draw the same salary.
Investors warned her that talent would flee, but she held to the egalitarian design.
Desks were assigned by lottery, and the intern's opinion in hiring counted like anyone's.
What mattered, she argued, was not generosity but standing: no one at the company ranked above anyone else.
Five years on, rivals still tease her about the flat pay scale, and she still answers that equal footing was the point.
